title: AI-Generated Menu Pictures Scare Customers Away
paragraphs: Many restaurants have started using artificial intelligence (AI) to create pictures of food for their menus and advertisements, because it is cheap and fast. However, many customers find these images strange or even disgusting, and some say the pictures actually make them less likely to order.

Examples of strange AI food images have gone viral on social media around the world. In Los Angeles, food stalls at a night market used AI-generated menu pictures, and one customer, Adaeze Onejeme, chose to buy from stalls that did not use them. She asked whether such pictures counted as false advertising. In Berlin, a billboard showed a quiche that looked like plastic, while in Kuala Lumpur, a picture of spaghetti looked more like yarn. In South Korea, people have shared AI menu photos of noodles clumped into geometric shapes. A 23-year-old in Seoul said that when he sees AI food photos on a delivery app, he expects the food to be lower quality, so he hesitates to order.

Why do these pictures put people off? Alexander Diel, a researcher at the University of Duisburg-Essen in Germany, has studied the question. In a 2025 study, his team found that people rated slightly imperfect AI food images as more "uncanny" and less pleasant than either clearly unrealistic or highly realistic images. In a later study, people said they were less willing to eat food shown in AI images, even though they judged it to be just as healthy. Diel believes such images may trigger feelings of disgust, which evolved to protect humans from unsafe food.

Restaurant owners say they use AI to save money, since professional food photography can be expensive. According to the US National Restaurant Association, 26% of restaurant owners use AI, mainly for marketing.

However, experts warn that this can backfire. Nancy Hopkins of the International Association of Culinary Professionals advises small businesses to take their own photos with smartphones instead. Similarly, Lee Eun-hee, a professor at Inha University in South Korea, recommends showing the real food to customers.
